Production Cost Savings and Operational Results. ................................................................... 30 ix This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 1 Introduction Electrifying transportation increases the share of energy service demand that can be supplied by low-carbon electricity (Mai et al. 2018; Murphy et al. 2021; Jenkins et al. 2021; Williams et al. 2021; Browning et al. 2023). The cost of supplying electric vehicle (EV) charging can be reduced if EV charging occurs in locations and at times of high variable generation or low electricity infrastructure utilization (Muratori and Mai 2020; Borlaug et al. 2021; Borlaug et al. 2020; Anwar et al. 2022). We refer to mechanisms for aligning EV charging with these low-cost times as EV managed charging (EVMC). Electric light-duty vehicles (LDVs) are especially well suited for EVMC because most are parked at least 95% of the time (Wood et al. 2023). Realizing the benefits of EVMC entails coordinating the charging of thousands to millions of vehicles to minimize charging costs while ensuring EV drivers can complete all desired trips. The numerous mechanisms for coordinating EV charging described in the literature generally fall into two high-level categories, which we refer to and compare as direct load control (DLC) and price- responsive dispatch. DLC directly schedules vehicle charging to achieve a desired aggregate response. For example, DLC can coordinate EV charging with availability of bulk power system supply-side resources, or to flatten peak electricity load.
